title: Microsoft Disputes Vance's 'Foreign Indentured Servants' Claim With Its Own H-1B Data
excerpt: In a Thursday-afternoon statement, the company said 80% of its H-1B filings last year were extensions for existing employees, not new hires; Vance says the fraud task force has opened multiple criminal investigations.
body:
• Microsoft pushed back on Vice President JD Vance's fraud accusations on Thursday, saying about 80% of its roughly 6,000 H-1B applications in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of current employees, not to hire new workers.
  • The company said its remaining filings for new employees were for people already legally in the United States and amounted to about 1% of its U.S. workforce, adding that it pays H-1B workers the same as comparable employees.
  • Vance said the administration's fraud task force has launched multiple criminal investigations into visa-program abuse; Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling vowed to cut off "the head of the snake."
  • What it means for you: the Labor Department is refusing to accept or process any new or pending PERM applications for Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata, Wipro, HCL and Capgemini. H-1B visas already held are not automatically canceled, but workers with pending green-card steps should speak to immigration counsel immediately.

Microsoft on Thursday afternoon disputed the Trump administration's accusation that it committed fraud through the H-1B visa program, releasing its own filing data hours after Vice President JD Vance accused the company of replacing laid-off Americans with what he called "foreign indentured servants."

According to a company statement reported by Nextgov/FCW and the Daily Caller News Foundation, about 80% of the roughly 6,000 H-1B visa applications Microsoft submitted in the last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of existing employees. "These were not to hire new people," the company said. The remaining filings for new employees were for individuals already legally in the United States who chose to join the company, and those hires equal about 1% of Microsoft's U.S. workforce.

Microsoft added that it pays H-1B employees the same as other employees doing comparable work, that its H-1B wages are among the highest of any filer, and that the vast majority of its U.S. employees are Americans.

The administration's case

The rebuttal landed hours after Vance announced the suspension at a White House fraud task force briefing. Vance accused Microsoft of the worst abuse in the country, saying the company laid off 6,000 U.S. workers while benefiting from 6,300 H-1B visas and nearly 3,000 green cards. "If you do the math, for every worker that Microsoft laid off, they replaced that worker with one and a half foreign indentured servants," Vance said, according to the Associated Press.

https://x.com/townhallcom/status/2108203774648991960

The facts behind that arithmetic are disputed. Newsmax noted that Vance's remarks did not establish that each visa or green card represented a new hire replacing a laid-off worker, and Microsoft's own July employee memo said its job cuts totaled around 4,800 roles, about 2.1% of its global workforce. The company also says most of its H-1B activity is routine paperwork for people already on its payroll.

The suspension targets PERM, the Labor Department's permanent labor certification process, which is the required first step for most employer-sponsored green cards. The eight named companies — Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services, Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini — can no longer file new PERM applications, and pending ones involving them will not be processed. The administration said the firms had requested almost 3 million foreign workers since 2009.

"We will not accept any new or process any pending permanent labor certification applications involving these companies."

— Keith Sonderling, Labor Secretary

Criminal investigations and federal contracts

Vance said the fraud task force has launched multiple criminal investigations into abuse of the foreign worker programs, but added that the abuse was so severe action could not wait. "We are cutting off the head of the snake," Sonderling said at the briefing, according to Nextgov.

The suspension may reach beyond the companies' commercial hiring. Many of the targeted firms are federal contractors: Microsoft is one of the government's largest software suppliers, and Cognizant, Capgemini, Infosys, Tata, Wipro and HCL perform federal IT services work directly or through U.S. subsidiaries. Nextgov reported it is not yet clear whether the suspension affects workers assigned to government contracts.

The administration is also scrutinizing nine universities, including Harvard, Yale, Stanford and Brown, over their use of foreign researchers, a probe announced at the same briefing.

Diaspora angle

The fight matters most to the tens of thousands of Indian professionals whose green-card prospects run through these eight companies. PERM is the bridge between an H-1B and permanent residency, and for workers already deep in decade-long backlogs, a freeze on new and pending applications can strand a case mid-process. Reuters noted that Meta, Amazon and Google remain free to participate in PERM, so the suspension is targeted rather than industry-wide — but for employees of the named firms, the practical advice is the same: do not assume your pending PERM is safe, and get immigration counsel before the next filing deadline.

There is also an irony the White House has not explained away: on the same day Vance called Microsoft the country's biggest abuser of the visa system, President Trump awarded Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella the National Medal of Technology and Innovation at the White House science summit.

What to watch

Three things will determine how far this goes. First, the criminal investigations: if the task force produces indictments, the story shifts from policy pressure to prosecutions. Second, the universities probe and the federal-contractor question will show whether the suspension is a contained enforcement action or the opening move of a broader campaign. Third, Microsoft's promised cooperation: the company said it looks forward to giving the administration more information, setting up a negotiation that could narrow or end the suspension. Economists warned of the opposite risk — Chad Sparber of Colgate told Reuters that keeping skilled foreign workers out does not protect American workers, because "they'll certainly compete with Americans by working abroad."
